stats_crv_density.description: Normalise a piecewise density, distinguish point probability from curve height and integrate over the actual support.

sections.title: What part of a density graph represents probability?
sections.label: Read area
sections.intro: A density is a height per unit of the variable. The probability of an interval is the area above it.

blocks.html: Use \(\mathrm P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm dx\). For a continuous distribution with a density, each single point has probability zero.

figure.alt: An increasing density from zero to one with a blue shaded interval between one quarter and three quarters.
figure.caption: The interval probability is the shaded area; the height at a single point contributes no area.

blocks.html: A height may exceed one. It is the area, after using the horizontal width, that must be between zero and one.

blocks.title: Distinguish a density height from an area
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{8 x}{5} + \frac{8}{5}\) for \(0\le x\le\frac{1}{2}\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the stated height at \(\frac{1}{8}\), the point probability \(\mathrm P(X=\frac{1}{8})\), and \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{8}\le X\le\frac{3}{8})\).

retry.feedback: That is the height of the density at the point. A point has no width.

blocks.hint: A height needs a width to contribute probability.
blocks.solution:
Substituting into the density gives a height of \(\frac{9}{5}\).

Any single point has zero probability in a continuous distribution with a density.

Integrate on the relevant support pieces to get \(\int_{\frac{1}{8}}^{\frac{3}{8}}\frac{8 x}{5} + \frac{8}{5}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).

sections.title: How do I choose the unknown scale?
sections.label: Normalise the whole support
sections.intro: Start with the entire area. Only after fixing the constant should you narrow the bounds to the event in question.

blocks.html: Multiply the proposed shape by a single constant so that the sum of all branch integrals is one.
Do not set the area of only the requested event equal to one.

blocks.title: Scale the full density before finding an interval probability
blocks.prompt:
The proposed density has the following non-zero pieces: \(k(3 - x)\) on \(0\le x<3\). It is zero elsewhere.

Find \(k\) and \(\mathrm P(1<X<2)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use the entire support to determine k, then restrict the probability calculation to the event.
blocks.solution:
The unscaled area is \(\int_{0}^{3}3 - x\,\mathrm dx=\frac{9}{2}\). The true area must be one.

Thus \(k=\frac{2}{9}\). Substituting this makes all densities non-negative on their stated intervals.

Use only the active pieces of the requested event. This gives \(\int_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{3} - \frac{2 x}{9}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{3}\).

sections.title: When must I split an interval integral?
sections.label: Split at every join
sections.intro: A piecewise model can have different equations on adjacent parts of one support. Use each equation only on its assigned interval.

blocks.html: A density may jump at a break. Unless the question adds a condition, the heights on the two sides need not be equal.
The formula for the first branch must stop where the second begins.

Event positionIntegral choice
Inside one branchOne integral on that interval.
Across a joinClip and sum the separate integrals.
Inside a gapProbability zero.

blocks.title: Scale the full density before finding an interval probability
blocks.prompt:
The proposed density has the following non-zero pieces: \(k(x + 1)\) on \(0\le x<2\); \(k(1)\) on \(2\le x<5\). It is zero elsewhere.

Find \(k\) and \(\mathrm P(1<X<3)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Use the entire support to determine k, then restrict the probability calculation to the event.
blocks.solution:
The unscaled area is \(\int_{0}^{2}x + 1\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{5}1\,\mathrm dx=7\). The true area must be one.

Thus \(k=\frac{1}{7}\). Substituting this makes all densities non-negative on their stated intervals.

Use only the active pieces of the requested event. This gives \(\int_{1}^{2}\frac{x}{7} + \frac{1}{7}\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{7}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).

sections.title: What does a gap in the support contribute?
sections.label: Skip empty intervals
sections.intro: An event can include values that the model never produces. Those intervals contribute no area.

blocks.html: Clip each event to the union of the stated support intervals. Add only the parts with non-zero density.
Do not bridge a gap by extending the nearest formula.

blocks.title: Find the probability across the relevant branches
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(-3\le x<-1\); \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(2\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(-2<X\le3)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Write the actual interval for each branch before integrating.
blocks.solution:
Clip the requested event to the support. At each change of formula start a separate integral.

The contributing areas give \(\int_{-2}^{-1}\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).

sections.title: Is a total area of one sufficient?
sections.label: Check area and sign
sections.intro: One condition controls the total area; a separate condition prevents negative probabilities.

blocks.html: A density needs \(f(x)\ge0\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,\mathrm dx=1\). Check both.
A negative section can cancel positive area in the total integral. That would still be invalid.

blocks.title: Check the two density requirements
blocks.prompt: A proposed density is \(2 x\) on \(0\le x\le1\) and zero elsewhere. Find the area under it on this interval. Then decide whether the model is a valid density.
blocks.hint: A total integral of one is necessary but insufficient if any branch has negative height.
blocks.solution:
The integral is \(\int_{0}^{1}2 x\,\mathrm dx=1\).

The least value on the proposed support is \(0\).

Both conditions hold.

sections.title: Can changing one endpoint alter a probability?
sections.label: Interpret endpoint types
sections.intro: Including or excluding a single boundary point does not affect a probability. The statement still determines which height is assigned at that boundary.

blocks.html: For interval probability, a formula can be changed at an isolated point without changing any area.
A jump in the height is allowed; it does not create a jump in cumulative probability.

blocks.title: Find the probability across the relevant branches
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(1\) for \(0\le x<\frac{1}{2}\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(2\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(\frac{3}{4}<X\le\frac{3}{2})\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Write the actual interval for each branch before integrating.
blocks.solution:
Clip the requested event to the support. At each change of formula start a separate integral.

The contributing areas give \(0=0\).

examples.title: Distinguish a density height from an area
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{5} + \frac{4}{5}\) for \(0\le x\le1\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the stated height at \(\frac{1}{4}\), the point probability \(\mathrm P(X=\frac{1}{4})\), and \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{4}\le X\le\frac{3}{4})\).
solution: Substituting into the density gives a height of \(\frac{9}{10}\).
Any single point has zero probability in a continuous distribution with a density.
Integrate on the relevant support pieces to get \(\int_{\frac{1}{4}}^{\frac{3}{4}}\frac{2 x}{5} + \frac{4}{5}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Distinguish a density height from an area

Find the stated height at \(\frac{1}{16}\), the point probability \(\mathrm P(X=\frac{1}{16})\), and \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{16}\le X\le\frac{1}{8})\).
solution: Substituting into the density gives a height of \(4\).
Any single point has zero probability in a continuous distribution with a density.
Integrate on the relevant support pieces to get \(\int_{\frac{1}{16}}^{\frac{1}{8}}4\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{4}\).

examples.title: Scale the full density before finding an interval probability
examples.question:
The proposed density has the following non-zero pieces: \(k(x + 2)\) on \(0\le x<1\). It is zero elsewhere.

Find \(k\) and \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{4}<X<\frac{3}{4})\) exactly.
solution: The unscaled area is \(\int_{0}^{1}x + 2\,\mathrm dx=\frac{5}{2}\). The true area must be one.
Thus \(k=\frac{2}{5}\). Substituting this makes all densities non-negative on their stated intervals.
Use only the active pieces of the requested event. This gives \(\int_{\frac{1}{4}}^{\frac{3}{4}}\frac{2 x}{5} + \frac{4}{5}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Find the probability across the relevant branches
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{5}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{2}{5}\) for \(1\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{2}<X\le2)\) exactly.
solution: Clip the requested event to the support. At each change of formula start a separate integral.
The contributing areas give \(\int_{\frac{1}{2}}^{1}\frac{2 x}{5}\,\mathrm dx+\int_{1}^{2}\frac{2}{5}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{11}{20}\).

examples.title: Find the probability across the relevant branches
examples.question:
The density is \(1\) for \(0\le x<\frac{1}{2}\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(2\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{4}<X\le\frac{5}{2})\) exactly.
solution: Clip the requested event to the support. At each change of formula start a separate integral.
The contributing areas give \(\int_{\frac{1}{4}}^{\frac{1}{2}}1\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{\frac{5}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Check the two density requirements
examples.question: A proposed density is \(3 x - \frac{1}{2}\) on \(0\le x\le1\) and zero elsewhere. Find the area under it on this interval. Then decide whether the model is a valid density.
solution: The integral is \(\int_{0}^{1}3 x - \frac{1}{2}\,\mathrm dx=1\).
The least value on the proposed support is \(- \frac{1}{2}\).
A valid density needs total area one and non-negative height throughout.

examples.title: Find the probability across the relevant branches
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{5}\) for \(-2\le x\le3\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(-2<X\le3)\) exactly.
solution: Clip the requested event to the support. At each change of formula start a separate integral.
The contributing areas give \(\int_{-2}^{3}\frac{1}{5}\,\mathrm dx=1\).

glossary.definition: A non-negative function whose area on an interval is its probability.
The region where a distribution can place probability. A gap has zero density.
Choose a constant which makes the total area one.
A single point has probability zero in a distribution with a density.

stats_crv_cdf.description: Build cumulative distribution functions, invert the correct branch for a quantile and use cumulative differences for conditional probabilities.

sections.title: What must a complete CDF include?
sections.label: Include exterior branches
sections.intro: Start below the support at zero, accumulate mass through the model, and finish at one after the support.

blocks.html: Write \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,\mathrm dt\). The integration variable is separate from the upper bound.
When a new branch starts, carry across the probability already accumulated.

blocks.title: Build the cumulative description from the full density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{9} + \frac{2}{9}\) for \(-1\le x\le2\) and zero elsewhere.

On paper, derive the complete CDF. Enter \(F(1)\) as an exact value.
blocks.hint: Start the first branch from zero and add the completed mass when you change branch.
blocks.solution:
Start each branch with all mass accumulated before its left endpoint. In an empty interval, that value stays fixed.

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<-1\\\frac{x^{2}}{9} + \frac{2 x}{9} + \frac{1}{9}&-1\le x<2\\1&x\ge2\end{cases}\]

At \(1\) the CDF is \(\frac{4}{9}\).

sections.title: Why is the CDF flat in a gap?
sections.label: Keep earlier mass during a gap
sections.intro: If density is zero on an interval, no additional probability accumulates there.

blocks.html: The CDF is continuous for a distribution with a density, even if the density jumps. Test the value at each join from both sides.

figure.alt: CDF rising from zero to one half between zero and two, flat from two to three, then increasing to one at four.
figure.caption: A flat part of the CDF records a gap in the support.

blocks.html: Zero density in a gap gives a constant cumulative probability rather than a reset to zero.

blocks.title: Build the cumulative description from the full density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(2\le x<5\) and zero elsewhere.

On paper, derive the complete CDF. Enter \(F(\frac{3}{2})\) as an exact value.
blocks.hint: Start the first branch from zero and add the completed mass when you change branch.
blocks.solution:
Start each branch with all mass accumulated before its left endpoint. In an empty interval, that value stays fixed.

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{x}{4}&0\le x<1\\\frac{1}{4}&1\le x<2\\\frac{x}{4} - \frac{1}{4}&2\le x<5\\1&x\ge5\end{cases}\]

At \(\frac{3}{2}\) the CDF is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

sections.title: How do I recover the density on a branch?
sections.label: Differentiate the CDF
sections.intro: Differentiate on the open interval where one formula applies. A corner marks a change of derivative, not a point mass.

blocks.html: Where the cumulative function is differentiable, \(f(x)=F^{\prime}(x)\). Constant sections give zero density.
The CDF value itself is an area, not the local density.

blocks.title: Recover a density from a cumulative function
blocks.prompt:
A continuous random variable has CDF

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{x}{4}&0\le x<2\\\frac{1}{2}&2\le x<3\\\frac{x}{2} - 1&3\le x<4\\1&x\ge4\end{cases}\]

Differentiate to find the density away from breakpoints. Enter the density value at \(\frac{5}{2}\).
blocks.hint: Differentiate the active branch, not its cumulative value.
blocks.solution:
On each open branch, differentiate the cumulative function. Constant branches give density zero.

The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x<2\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(3\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

The expression in force at \(\frac{5}{2}\) gives \(0\).

sections.title: Which part of the CDF reaches the target?
sections.label: Match level before solving
sections.intro: Compare the target with the CDF levels at the breakpoints. Then solve the equation on the first branch that reaches it.

blocks.html: For level \(p\), use the smallest input with \(F(x)\ge p\). A plateau may give several solutions to \(F(x)=p\).
Check that the root lies on the chosen branch and use the left end of a plateau when the lower quantile is requested.

blocks.title: Solve on the cumulative branch that reaches the target
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{x}{8}\) for \(0\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the lower quantile at level \(\frac{1}{4}\). Use the earliest input where the cumulative probability reaches the target.
blocks.hint: Compare the target with the cumulative masses at the breakpoints before solving.
blocks.solution:
On the first branch reaching \(\frac{1}{4}\), the input lies between \(0\) and \(4\).

\[\frac{x^{2}}{16}=\frac{1}{4}\]

The first qualifying input is \(2\). An equal cumulative value later on a flat branch would not change the lower quantile.

sections.title: How do cumulative values give a conditional tail?
sections.label: Use the full condition event
sections.intro: When the upper target lies inside the conditioning tail, its probability is also the overlap probability.

blocks.html: For \(a<b\), \(\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)=\frac{1-F(b)}{1-F(a)}\) if \(F(a)<1\).
Subtract from one for a tail. A CDF value is a lower cumulative probability.

blocks.title: Use the overlap in a conditional upper tail
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x<2\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(3\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(X>\frac{7}{2}\mid X>\frac{1}{2})\) exactly.

retry.feedback: That is the overlap probability. Divide it by the full condition probability.

blocks.hint: The denominator is all of the condition event, including the part outside the target.
blocks.solution:
The condition has probability \(\frac{7}{8}\). The target is already inside that condition and has probability \(\frac{1}{4}\).

Divide the overlap by the conditioning probability: \(\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{7}{8}}=\frac{2}{7}\).

sections.title: Can the two quartiles come from different branches?
sections.label: Calculate both thresholds
sections.intro: Solve the two level equations separately. Subtract the lower quantile from the upper quantile only after selecting each branch.

blocks.html: The interquartile range is a distance on the horizontal scale. It is not the gap between 25 per cent and 75 per cent on the vertical scale.
Do not invert a branch outside its own input interval.

blocks.title: Find quartiles on their appropriate branches
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{8}\) for \(1\le x\le9\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range.
blocks.hint: Find the two quartiles separately; the two branches need not be the same.
blocks.solution:
The lower quartile is the first value where the CDF reaches \(\frac{1}{4}\); here it is \(3\). The upper quartile is the first value where it reaches \(\frac{3}{4}\); here it is \(7\).

\[\frac{x}{8} - \frac{1}{8}=\frac{1}{4}\]\[\frac{x}{8} - \frac{1}{8}=\frac{3}{4}\]

Their difference is \(4\).

examples.title: Build the cumulative description from the full density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{x}{3} + \frac{1}{6}\) for \(0\le x\le2\) and zero elsewhere.

On paper, derive the complete CDF. Enter \(F(\frac{3}{2})\) as an exact value.
solution: Start each branch with all mass accumulated before its left endpoint. In an empty interval, that value stays fixed.
\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{x^{2}}{6} + \frac{x}{6}&0\le x<2\\1&x\ge2\end{cases}\]
At \(\frac{3}{2}\) the CDF is \(\frac{5}{8}\).

examples.title: Build the cumulative description from the full density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{6 x}{7}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{2}{7}\) for \(1\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.

On paper, derive the complete CDF. Enter \(F(2)\) as an exact value.
solution: Start each branch with all mass accumulated before its left endpoint. In an empty interval, that value stays fixed.
\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{3 x^{2}}{7}&0\le x<1\\\frac{2 x}{7} + \frac{1}{7}&1\le x<3\\1&x\ge3\end{cases}\]
At \(2\) the CDF is \(\frac{5}{7}\).

examples.title: Build the cumulative description from the full density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x<2\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(3\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

On paper, derive the complete CDF. Enter \(F(\frac{5}{2})\) as an exact value.
solution: Start each branch with all mass accumulated before its left endpoint. In an empty interval, that value stays fixed.
\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{x}{4}&0\le x<2\\\frac{1}{2}&2\le x<3\\\frac{x}{2} - 1&3\le x<4\\1&x\ge4\end{cases}\]
At \(\frac{5}{2}\) the CDF is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Recover a density from a cumulative function
examples.question:
A continuous random variable has CDF

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{3 x^{2}}{7}&0\le x<1\\\frac{2 x}{7} + \frac{1}{7}&1\le x<3\\1&x\ge3\end{cases}\]

Differentiate to find the density away from breakpoints. Enter the density value at \(\frac{3}{2}\).
solution: On each open branch, differentiate the cumulative function. Constant branches give density zero.
The density is \(\frac{6 x}{7}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{2}{7}\) for \(1\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.
The expression in force at \(\frac{3}{2}\) gives \(\frac{2}{7}\).

examples.title: Solve on the cumulative branch that reaches the target
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x<2\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(3\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the lower quantile at level \(\frac{1}{2}\). Use the earliest input where the cumulative probability reaches the target.
solution: On the first branch reaching \(\frac{1}{2}\), the input lies between \(0\) and \(2\).
The first qualifying input is \(2\). An equal cumulative value later on a flat branch would not change the lower quantile.

examples.title: Use the overlap in a conditional upper tail
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{x}{3} + \frac{1}{6}\) for \(0\le x\le2\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(X>\frac{3}{2}\mid X>\frac{1}{2})\) exactly.
solution: The condition has probability \(\frac{7}{8}\). The target is already inside that condition and has probability \(\frac{3}{8}\).
Divide the overlap by the conditioning probability: \(\frac{\frac{3}{8}}{\frac{7}{8}}=\frac{3}{7}\).

examples.title: Find quartiles on their appropriate branches
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x<2\); \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(3\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range.
solution: The lower quartile is the first value where the CDF reaches \(\frac{1}{4}\); here it is \(1\). The upper quartile is the first value where it reaches \(\frac{3}{4}\); here it is \(\frac{7}{2}\).
Their difference is \(\frac{5}{2}\).

A threshold where the cumulative probability reaches a given level.
A flat interval in the CDF, indicating an interval of zero probability.
The overlap divided by the full probability of the condition.

extraPractice.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{6 x}{7}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{2}{7}\) for \(1\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.

On paper, derive the complete CDF. Enter \(F(\frac{3}{2})\) as an exact value.
extraPractice.hint: Start the first branch from zero and add the completed mass when you change branch.
extraPractice.solution:
Start each branch with all mass accumulated before its left endpoint. In an empty interval, that value stays fixed.

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<0\\\frac{3 x^{2}}{7}&0\le x<1\\\frac{2 x}{7} + \frac{1}{7}&1\le x<3\\1&x\ge3\end{cases}\]

At \(\frac{3}{2}\) the CDF is \(\frac{4}{7}\).

extraPractice.title: Recover a density from a cumulative function
extraPractice.prompt:
A continuous random variable has CDF

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0&x<1\\\frac{x^{2}}{9} - \frac{2 x}{9} + \frac{1}{9}&1\le x<4\\1&x\ge4\end{cases}\]

Differentiate to find the density away from breakpoints. Enter the density value at \(2\).
extraPractice.hint: Differentiate the active branch, not its cumulative value.
extraPractice.solution:
On each open branch, differentiate the cumulative function. Constant branches give density zero.

The density is \(\frac{2 x}{9} - \frac{2}{9}\) for \(1\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

The expression in force at \(2\) gives \(\frac{2}{9}\).

extraPractice.title: Solve on the cumulative branch that reaches the target
extraPractice.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{5}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{1}{5}\) for \(2\le x<6\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the lower quantile at level \(\frac{1}{5}\). Use the earliest input where the cumulative probability reaches the target.
extraPractice.hint: Compare the target with the cumulative masses at the breakpoints before solving.
extraPractice.solution:
On the first branch reaching \(\frac{1}{5}\), the input lies between \(0\) and \(1\).

\[\frac{x}{5}=\frac{1}{5}\]

The first qualifying input is \(1\). An equal cumulative value later on a flat branch would not change the lower quantile.

extraPractice.title: Use the overlap in a conditional upper tail
extraPractice.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{25}\) for \(0\le x\le5\) and zero elsewhere.

Find \(\mathrm P(X>3\mid X>1)\) exactly.

retry.feedback: That is the overlap probability. Divide it by the full condition probability.

extraPractice.hint: The denominator is all of the condition event, including the part outside the target.
extraPractice.solution:
The condition has probability \(\frac{24}{25}\). The target is already inside that condition and has probability \(\frac{16}{25}\).

Divide the overlap by the conditioning probability: \(\frac{\frac{16}{25}}{\frac{24}{25}}=\frac{2}{3}\).

extraPractice.title: Find quartiles on their appropriate branches
extraPractice.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{8}\) for \(-4\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

Find the lower quartile, upper quartile and interquartile range.
extraPractice.hint: Find the two quartiles separately; the two branches need not be the same.
extraPractice.solution:
The lower quartile is the first value where the CDF reaches \(\frac{1}{4}\); here it is \(-2\). The upper quartile is the first value where it reaches \(\frac{3}{4}\); here it is \(2\).

\[\frac{x}{8} + \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{4}\]\[\frac{x}{8} + \frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{4}\]

Their difference is \(4\).

sections.title: Why is a continuous mean an integral?
sections.label: Weight the values by density
sections.intro: A mean averages possible values using their probabilities. The integral replaces the discrete weighted sum.

blocks.html: Use \(\mathrm E(X)=\int x f(x)\,\mathrm dx\) across every active support piece.
Integrating the density by itself gives total probability, not a mean.

blocks.title: Find moments without transforming the density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{x}{8}\) for \(0\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X\). Find the mean of Y. Give exact values.
blocks.hint: Integrate the requested function against the original density. For variance use the square of the same function in the second moment.
blocks.solution: Use the original density against \(x\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{0}^{4}\frac{x^{2}}{8}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{8}{3}\).

sections.title: Which square goes into the variance?
sections.label: Compute moments separately
sections.intro: Find the second moment by weighting each squared value. Separately square the first moment. Those are two different operations.

blocks.html: \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathrm E(X^2)-[\mathrm E(X)]^2\). The result cannot be negative.
The second moment alone does not measure the spread around the mean.

QuantityIntegrand
Mean\(xf(x)\)
Second moment\(x^2f(x)\)
Variance\((x-\mu)^2f(x)\) or subtract using the two moments.

blocks.title: Find moments without transforming the density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{3}\) for \(1\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X\). Find the mean and variance of Y. Give exact values.

retry.feedback: That is the second moment. Subtract the square of the mean.

blocks.hint: Integrate the requested function against the original density. For variance use the square of the same function in the second moment.
blocks.solution:
Use the original density against \(x\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{1}^{4}\frac{x}{3}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{5}{2}\).

For the second moment integrate \(x^{2}\) against the same density. This gives \(7\).

Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(\frac{3}{4}\).

sections.title: Do I need to transform the density first?
sections.label: Use the original density
sections.intro: For an expectation of a function, integrate that function of the original input. No inverse is needed, even when the function turns.

blocks.html: \(\mathrm E(g(X))=\int g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx\). The density still describes X.
In general the mean of the function is different from the function of the mean.

blocks.title: Find moments without transforming the density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{3}\) for \(-1\le x\le2\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X^{2}\). Find the mean and variance of Y. Give exact values.

retry.feedback: That is the second moment. Subtract the square of the mean.

blocks.hint: Integrate the requested function against the original density. For variance use the square of the same function in the second moment.
blocks.solution:
Use the original density against \(x^{2}\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{-1}^{2}\frac{x^{2}}{3}\,\mathrm dx=1\).

For the second moment integrate \(x^{4}\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{11}{5}\).

Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(\frac{6}{5}\).

sections.title: When can I use the linear short cut?
sections.label: Shift and scale
sections.intro: Linearity makes a change of origin or scale easier. A shift moves the mean but does not change the spread.

blocks.html: \(\mathrm E(aX+b)=a\mathrm E(X)+b\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
Multiply the variance by the square of the scale, even when the scale is negative.

blocks.title: Find moments without transforming the density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(1\le x\le3\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=2 X + 5\). Find the mean and variance of Y. Give exact values.

retry.feedback: That is the second moment. Subtract the square of the mean.

blocks.hint: Integrate the requested function against the original density. For variance use the square of the same function in the second moment.
blocks.solution:
Use the original density against \(2 x + 5\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{1}^{3}x + \frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm dx=9\).

For the second moment integrate \(4 x^{2} + 20 x + 25\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{247}{3}\).

Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(\frac{4}{3}\).

sections.title: How do several support pieces change the calculation?
sections.label: Add moment contributions
sections.intro: For each piece use its own density and its own interval. Add the separate contributions to a global moment.

blocks.html: For variance take the square of the global mean. Each part contributes to both integrals.
Do not average the variances of the pieces without including differences in their means.

blocks.title: Find moments without transforming the density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{3}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{2}{3}\) for \(2\le x<3\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X^{2}\). Find the mean and variance of Y. Give exact values.

retry.feedback: That is the second moment. Subtract the square of the mean.

blocks.hint: Integrate the requested function against the original density. For variance use the square of the same function in the second moment.
blocks.solution:
Use the original density against \(x^{2}\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{0}^{1}\frac{x^{2}}{3}\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{3}\frac{2 x^{2}}{3}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{13}{3}\).

For the second moment integrate \(x^{4}\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{141}{5}\).

Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(\frac{424}{45}\).

sections.title: What should I check before integrating a reciprocal?
sections.label: Check a lower endpoint
sections.intro: A reciprocal may require a separate convergence check when its original support reaches zero. Here choose a model whose lower endpoint is positive.

blocks.html: Use the correct power in the second moment. Keep the logarithm exact through the calculation, then round only if requested.
The reciprocal of the mean rarely gives the mean of the reciprocal.

blocks.title: Find moments without transforming the density
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{x}{6}\) for \(2\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=\frac{1}{X}\). Find the mean and variance of Y. Give results to 4 decimal places.
blocks.hint: Integrate the requested function against the original density. For variance use the square of the same function in the second moment.
blocks.solution:
Use the original density against \(\frac{1}{x}\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{6}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{3}\).

For the second moment integrate \(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{\log{\left(2 \right)}}{6}\).

Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(- \frac{1}{9} + \frac{\log{\left(2 \right)}}{6}\), which is \(0.0044\) to the requested accuracy.

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{3 x^{2}}{8}\) for \(0\le x\le2\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X\). Find the mean of Y. Give exact values.
solution: Use the original density against \(x\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{0}^{2}\frac{3 x^{3}}{8}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{3}{2}\).
Only the interval from \(0\) to \(2\) contributes. The antiderivative is \(\frac{3x^4}{32}\), which gives \(\mathbb E(Y)=\frac32\) after substituting both limits.

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{5}\) for \(-2\le x\le3\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X\). Find the mean of Y. Give exact values.
solution: Use the original density against \(x\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{-2}^{3}\frac{x}{5}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).
The antiderivative is \(\frac{x^2}{10}\), so the integral gives \(\frac{9-4}{10}=\frac12\). The density is uniform, and the interval midpoint confirms this mean.

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density

The density is \(\frac{3 x^{2}}{8}\) for \(0\le x\le2\) and zero elsewhere.

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

solution: Use the original density against \(\left(x - 2\right)^{2}\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{0}^{4}\frac{\left(x - 2\right)^{2}}{4}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{4}{3}\).
For the second moment integrate \(x^{4} - 8 x^{3} + 24 x^{2} - 32 x + 16\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{16}{5}\).
Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(\frac{64}{45}\).

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density

The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(0\le x\le4\) and zero elsewhere.

For the second moment integrate \(4 x^{2} - 12 x + 9\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{19}{3}\).

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{1}{2}\) for \(0\le x<1\); \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(2\le x<4\) and zero elsewhere.

solution: Use the original density against \(x\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{0}^{1}\frac{x}{2}\,\mathrm dx+\int_{2}^{4}\frac{x}{4}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{7}{4}\).

examples.title: Find moments without transforming the density
examples.question:
The density is \(\frac{x}{4}\) for \(1\le x\le3\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=\frac{1}{X}\). Find the mean and variance of Y. Give results to 4 decimal places.
solution: Use the original density against \(\frac{1}{x}\). The integral for the mean is \(\int_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm dx=\frac{1}{2}\).
For the second moment integrate \(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\) against the same density. This gives \(\frac{\log{\left(3 \right)}}{4}\).
Subtract the square of the mean to obtain \(- \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\log{\left(3 \right)}}{4}\), which is \(0.0247\) to the requested accuracy.

stats_crv_monotone.description: Map the support, invert increasing or decreasing events and differentiate a complete transformed CDF.

sections.title: Where does the new support start and end?
sections.label: Map both endpoints
sections.intro: Start with the image of the original support. On a monotone branch its two endpoints map to the two endpoints of the new range.

blocks.html: For an increasing transformation the order stays the same. State \(G=0\) below the support and \(G=1\) after it.

figure.alt: An upper number line shows endpoints 0 and 1 for X. They map to 1 and 3 on a lower Y number line.
figure.caption: Apply the transformation to both endpoints before considering CDF values inside the range.

blocks.html: Retaining the original bounds can give probabilities which are zero or one at the wrong inputs.

blocks.title: Transform the event before differentiating
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{15} + \frac{2}{15}\) for \(0\le x\le3\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=2 X - 2\). On paper, find its support and cumulative function. Enter \(G(1)\) and the density at \(1\) exactly.

retry.feedback: This is the accumulated probability. The density is its derivative on the active branch.

blocks.hint: Map both endpoints first. If the transformation decreases, reverse the inequality and use a tail.
blocks.solution:
The new range extends from \(-2\) to \(4\). In its interior, \(Y\le y\) is equivalent to \(X\le\frac{y}{2} + 1\).

Use the original CDF at the inverse input.

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<-2\\\frac{y^{2}}{60} + \frac{2 y}{15} + \frac{1}{5}&-2\le y<4\\1&y\ge4\end{cases}\]

Differentiate inside each branch to recover the density.

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{y}{30} + \frac{2}{15}&-2<y<4\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\]

At the requested point the cumulative value is \(\frac{7}{20}\) and the density is \(\frac{1}{6}\).

sections.title: What event does a nonlinear increasing map create?
sections.label: Invert an increasing inequality
sections.intro: Write the event in the new variable first. On an increasing branch inversion preserves the direction of the inequality.

blocks.html: If \(h\) is increasing and one-to-one on the support, \(G(y)=F_X(h^{-1}(y))\) for interior y.
Take the inverse which lies on the stated support. A second algebraic root outside it has no probability.

blocks.title: Transform the event before differentiating
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{21}\) for \(2\le x\le5\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X^{2} + 3\). On paper, find its support and cumulative function. Enter \(G(12)\) and the density at \(12\) exactly.

retry.feedback: This is the accumulated probability. The density is its derivative on the active branch.

blocks.hint: Map both endpoints first. If the transformation decreases, reverse the inequality and use a tail.
blocks.solution:
The new range extends from \(7\) to \(28\). In its interior, \(Y\le y\) is equivalent to \(X\le\sqrt{y - 3}\).

Use the original CDF at the inverse input.

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<7\\\frac{y}{21} - \frac{1}{3}&7\le y<28\\1&y\ge28\end{cases}\]

Differentiate inside each branch to recover the density.

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{21}&7<y<28\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\]

At the requested point the cumulative value is \(\frac{5}{21}\) and the density is \(\frac{1}{21}\).

sections.title: Why does a decreasing inverse use a tail?
sections.label: Reverse the inequality
sections.intro: As the original input grows, the transformed value decreases. A lower event in Y corresponds to an upper event in X.

blocks.html: For decreasing \(h\), use \(G(y)=1-F_X(h^{-1}(y))\). The equality endpoint has no probability mass.
Subtract from one to obtain the tail and reverse the order of the mapped endpoints.

blocks.title: Transform the event before differentiating
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{x}{4}\) for \(1\le x\le3\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=\frac{6}{X}\). On paper, find its support and cumulative function. Enter \(G(3)\) and the density at \(3\) exactly.

retry.feedback: This is the accumulated probability. The density is its derivative on the active branch.

blocks.hint: Map both endpoints first. If the transformation decreases, reverse the inequality and use a tail.
blocks.solution:
The new range extends from \(2\) to \(6\). In its interior, \(Y\le y\) is equivalent to \(X\ge\frac{6}{y}\).

Use the upper tail at the inverse input.

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<2\\\frac{9}{8} - \frac{9}{2 y^{2}}&2\le y<6\\1&y\ge6\end{cases}\]

Differentiate inside each branch to recover the density.

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{9}{y^{3}}&2<y<6\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\]

At the requested point the cumulative value is \(\frac{5}{8}\) and the density is \(\frac{1}{3}\).

sections.title: What must happen when I differentiate the transformed CDF?
sections.label: Include the chain factor
sections.intro: Differentiate the interior CDF with respect to the new variable. Its formula contains the inverse.

blocks.html: On a monotone branch the transformed density is \(f_X(h^{-1}(y))\lvert (h^{-1})^{\prime}(y)\rvert\). This verifies the CDF derivation.
Substituting into the old density gives only one factor. A stretching of the axis changes the density needed to preserve area.

TransformationEvent for interior y
Increasing\(X\le h^{-1}(y)\)
Decreasing\(X\ge h^{-1}(y)\)

blocks.title: Transform the event before differentiating
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{x}{8} + \frac{3}{8}\) for \(-3\le x\le1\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=3 - 2 X\). On paper, find its support and cumulative function. Enter \(G(5)\) and the density at \(5\) exactly.

retry.feedback: This is the accumulated probability. The density is its derivative on the active branch.

blocks.hint: Map both endpoints first. If the transformation decreases, reverse the inequality and use a tail.
blocks.solution:
The new range extends from \(1\) to \(9\). In its interior, \(Y\le y\) is equivalent to \(X\ge\frac{3}{2} - \frac{y}{2}\).

Use the upper tail at the inverse input.

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<1\\- \frac{y^{2}}{64} + \frac{9 y}{32} - \frac{17}{64}&1\le y<9\\1&y\ge9\end{cases}\]

Differentiate inside each branch to recover the density.

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{9}{32} - \frac{y}{32}&1<y<9\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\]

At the requested point the cumulative value is \(\frac{3}{4}\) and the density is \(\frac{1}{8}\).

sections.title: Which percentile does a decreasing map transport?
sections.label: Use the complementary level
sections.intro: A percentile moves through an increasing transformation at the same cumulative level. A strictly decreasing transformation interchanges lower and upper ordering.

blocks.html: If the original distribution is continuous and strictly increasing over its support, use level \(p\) for an increasing map and \(1-p\) for a decreasing map.
A median stays at level one half, but other percentiles generally change level when the map decreases.

blocks.title: Transport a percentile through a monotone map
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{1}{4}\) for \(1\le x\le5\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=X^{2}\). Find the lower quantile of Y at level \(\frac{1}{4}\).

blocks.title: Transform the event before differentiating
blocks.prompt:
The density is \(\frac{2 x}{21}\) for \(2\le x\le5\) and zero elsewhere.

Let \(Y=\frac{4}{X}\). On paper, find its support and cumulative function. Enter \(G(1)\) and the density at \(1\) exactly.

retry.feedback: This is the accumulated probability. The density is its derivative on the active branch.

blocks.hint: Map both endpoints first. If the transformation decreases, reverse the inequality and use a tail.
blocks.solution:
The new range extends from \(\frac{4}{5}\) to \(2\). In its interior, \(Y\le y\) is equivalent to \(X\ge\frac{4}{y}\).

Use the upper tail at the inverse input.

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0&y<\frac{4}{5}\\\frac{25}{21} - \frac{16}{21 y^{2}}&\frac{4}{5}\le y<2\\1&y\ge2\end{cases}\]

Differentiate inside each branch to recover the density.

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{32}{21 y^{3}}&\frac{4}{5}<y<2\\0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\]

At the requested point the cumulative value is \(\frac{3}{7}\) and the density is \(\frac{32}{21}\).

At the requested point the cumulative value is \(\frac{1}{2}\) and the density is \(\frac{3}{4}\).
